items: 1Define sequences and series — distinguish a finite series from an infinite series, and tell an Arithmetic Progression apart from a Geometric Progression.
2Apply the nth-term and sum formulas for both AP and GP, including setting up and solving simultaneous equations to find the first term a and common difference/ratio when they are not given directly.
3Evaluate the sum to infinity of a convergent geometric series, and apply progressions to real-world problems such as salary growth and asset depreciation.

blocks.x: Core definitions

Sequence A set of numbers (terms) written in a defined order with a rule or formula for obtaining each term. For example, 1, 3, 5, 7, \ldots and 2, 4, 6, 8, \ldots are all sequences. Each term is obtained by adding 2 to the preceding term.

Series Formed when the terms of a sequence are added. For example, 2+4+6+8+\ldots and 1+3+5+7+\ldots are all series. If a series stops after a finite number of terms it is called a finite series; if it does not terminate it is said to be infinite.

Arithmetic Progression (AP) Also called a Linear Progression or Linear Sequence — a sequence in which any term differs from the preceding term by a constant called the common difference (d), which may be positive or negative. For example, 2,4,6,8,\ldots has a common difference of 2.

Geometric Progression (GP) Also called an Exponential Progression or Exponential Sequence — a sequence where each term is obtained by multiplying the preceding term by a constant called the common ratio (r). For instance, 2,4,8,16,\ldots is a GP with common ratio 2.
Sequence→ Series→ AP or GP?→ nth term (un)→ Sum (Sn)→ Real-world application

sections.title: The general (nth) term of a linear sequence

blocks.x: Linear sequences
An AP is a sequence in which any term differs from the preceding term by a constant common difference, d, which may be positive or negative.
The general (nth) term of a linear sequence
un = a + (n−1)d or l = a + (n−1)d un = the nth term of the sequence • l = last term • a = first term • d = common difference • n = number of terms d = un − un−1 or d = un+1 − un
Finding the nth term
Find the 11th term of the sequence 4, 9, 14, 19, …

items: 1Read off the first term and find the common difference by subtracting consecutive terms.a = 4; d = 9 − 4 = 14 − 9 = 5
2Write the general term formula and substitute n = 11.u<sub>n</sub> = a + (n−1)d ⇒ u<sub>11</sub> = 4 + (11−1) × 5
3Simplify.u<sub>11</sub> = 4 + 10 × 5 = 4 + 50

blocks.x: u<sub>11</sub> = 54
The fourth term of a linear sequence is 19 and the eleventh term is 54. Find the eighth term.

items: 1Express both given terms using the general formula, forming two simultaneous equations.u<sub>4</sub> = a + 3d = 19 …(1) u<sub>11</sub> = a + 10d = 54 …(2)
2Subtract (1) from (2) to eliminate a and solve for d.(a + 10d) − (a + 3d) = 54 − 19 ⇒ 7d = 35 ⇒ d = 5
3Substitute d back into equation (1) to find a.a + 15 = 19 ⇒ a = 4
4Use a and d to compute the eighth term.u<sub>8</sub> = a + (8−1)d = 4 + (7)(5) = 4 + 35

blocks.x: u<sub>8</sub> = 39

blocks.x: Sum of an AP

S<sub>n</sub> = n2[2a + (n−1)d] or S<sub>n</sub> = n2(a + l)
where l = a + (n−1)d is the last term. The first formula is used when a and d are known; the second is used when a and l are known but not the common difference.
Find the sum of the first 15 terms of the sequence 5, 9, 13, 17, …

items: 1Identify a, d and n.a = 5, d = 9 − 5 = 4, n = 15
2Substitute into the sum formula.S<sub>n</sub> = n2[2a + (n−1)d] ⇒ S<sub>15</sub> = 152[2(5) + (14)4]
3Simplify the bracket, then multiply out.S<sub>15</sub> = 152[66]

blocks.x: Find the number of terms of the linear sequence 5, 8, 11, 14, … which has a sum of 1025.

items: 1Identify a and d, and set the sum formula equal to 1025.a = 5, d = 8−5 = 3; S<sub>n</sub> = n2[2a+(n−1)d] = 1025
2Multiply both sides by 2 and substitute a, d.2(1025) = n[2(5) + (n−1)(3)] ⇒ 2050 = n[10 + (n−1)(3)]
3Expand and collect into a quadratic in n.2050 = 10n + 3n² − 3n ⇒ 3n² + 7n − 2050 = 0
5Reject the negative root — a number of terms cannot be negative.n = 150/6 = 25 (the root n = −164/6 is rejected)

sections.title: The general (nth) term of a GP

blocks.x: Exponential sequences
A GP is a sequence where each term is obtained by multiplying a preceding term by a constant factor called the common ratio, r.
The general (nth) term of a GP

u<sub>n</sub> = ar<sup>n−1</sup>
where r = u<sub>n</sub>u<sub>n−1</sub> = u<sub>n+1</sub>u<sub>n</sub>. For instance, 2, 4, 8, 16, … is a GP with common ratio r = 2.
Finding the nth term
Find the seventh term of the exponential sequence 5, 10, 20, …

items: 1Identify the first term and common ratio.a = 5; r = 105 = 2
2Substitute into the general term formula with n = 7.u<sub>n</sub> = ar<sup>n−1</sup> ⇒ u<sub>7</sub> = 5 × 2<sup>6</sup>
3Evaluate the power and multiply.u<sub>7</sub> = 5 × 64

blocks.x: u<sub>7</sub> = 320
Find the 12th term of the GP 128, 64, 32, …

items: 1Identify a and r.a = 128; r = 64128 = 12
2Substitute into u<sub>n</sub> = ar<sup>n−1</sup> with n = 12.u<sub>12</sub> = 128 × (12)<sup>11</sup>
3Rewrite both factors as powers of 2 and combine indices.u<sub>12</sub> = 2<sup>7</sup> × 2<sup>−11</sup> = 2<sup>−4</sup>

blocks.x: Sum of a GP

S<sub>n</sub> = a(1−r<sup>n</sup>)1−r, |r| < 1 or S<sub>n</sub> = a(r<sup>n</sup>−1)r−1, |r| > 1
|r| < 1 implies −1 < r < 1; |r| > 1 implies either r < −1 or r > 1.
Find the sum of the first 13 terms of the GP 12, 14, 18, …

items: 1Identify a and r.a = 12; r = 14 ÷ 12 = 12
2Since |r| < 1, use S<sub>n</sub> = a(1−r<sup>n</sup>)/(1−r) with n = 13.S<sub>13</sub> = 12·(1−(12)<sup>13</sup>) ÷ (1−12)
3Evaluate numerically.S<sub>13</sub> = 12·(1−(12)<sup>13</sup>) ÷ (12)

blocks.x: Sum to infinity of a GP
When |r| < 1, S<sub>n</sub> = a(1−r<sup>n</sup>)/(1−r) = a/(1−r) − ar<sup>n</sup>/(1−r). As n → ∞, r<sup>n</sup> → 0, so ar<sup>n</sup>/(1−r) → 0 as n → ∞. Therefore:
S<sub>∞</sub> = a1−r
Find the sum to infinity of 710 + 7100 + 71000 + …

items: 1Identify a and r from the series.a = 710; r = (7100) ÷ (710) = 110
2Substitute into the sum-to-infinity formula.S<sub>∞</sub> = a1−r = 7/101−1/10 = 7/109/10
3Simplify the complex fraction.S<sub>∞</sub> = 79

blocks.x: Problem solving
Progressions model real situations that change by a constant amount (AP) or a constant factor (GP) each period — such as a rising salary or a depreciating asset.
Application of sequence — salary growth
A man's salary increases by GH¢8,000 each year. If his total salary at the end of 12 years is GH¢18,525,000, find (a) his initial salary and (b) his salary in the 12th year.

items: 1Recognise this as an AP: the salary changes by a constant amount each year, so d = 8,000. We are given S<sub>12</sub> and n.d = 8,000; S<sub>12</sub> = 18,525,000; n = 12
2Substitute into the sum formula for an AP.S<sub>n</sub> = n2[2a+(n−1)d] ⇒ 18,525,000 = 122[2a + (11)(8,000)]
4Divide to find the initial salary a.a = 1,499,750
5Use u<sub>n</sub> = a + (n−1)d to find the salary in the 12th year.u<sub>12</sub> = a + 11d = 1,499,750 + 11(8,000) = 1,499,750 + 88,000

blocks.x: Initial salary a = GH¢1,499,750 · u<sub>12</sub> = GH¢1,587,750
Depreciation — an exponential-sequence scenario

Just as a salary that grows by a fixed amount each year is an AP, an asset that loses a fixed percentage of its value each year forms a GP: each year's value is the previous year's value multiplied by a constant ratio r = 1 − (\text{rate}). This is the exact structure behind the trial problem below.
Trial — try it yourself

items: The value of a car originally valued at GH¢30,000,000 depreciates by 15% per annum (so r = 0.85 each year, forming a GP with a = 30,000,000). Calculate its value after 5 years. The car is sold when its value is less than GH¢5,500,000 — after how many years was the car sold?
